sentences.text: Gualicho is described as a medium-sized theropod with strong, agile legs and reduced arms with only two functional fingers.
The animal measured between 6 and 7 meters in length and 1.70 meters in height.
While it possessed reduced arms with possibly two functional fingers, a 2020 study suggests a third finger may have been present.
The genus name Gualicho is derived from the gualichu, a demon from local folklore.
The specific name shinyae honors Akiko Shinya, the discoverer of the specimen.
It coexisted with giants like Mapusaurus and Argentinosaurus in a warm environment featuring large rivers.
The holotype skeleton of Gualicho was discovered on February 13, 2007, by Akiko Shinya near the Ezequiel Ramos Mexía Reservoir.
Gualicho was formally named and described in 2016 by Sebastián Apesteguía, Nathan D. Smith, Rubén Juárez Valieri, and Peter J. Makovicky.
The holotype specimen, MPCN PV 0001, is a partial skeleton that lacks the skull.
Many bones of the holotype were found in their original anatomical positions, though much of the skeleton was destroyed by erosion.
If Gualicho is considered a carnosaur, its two functional fingers might indicate convergent evolution of limb reduction similar to tyrannosaurids and abelisaurids.
A 2016 analysis by Apesteguía et al. placed Gualicho within the clade Carcharodontosauria.
Gualicho is classified within the unranked family Neotheropoda.
Gualicho belongs to the unranked genus Averostra.
The parent group for the genus Gualicho is Tyrannosauroidea.
Gualicho is classified in the class Reptilia.
Because Gualicho's humerus shares similarities with various groups of ceratosaurs, researchers cannot assign the animal to a specific theropod clade with certainty.
Gualicho lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 106 million years ago.
Gualicho lived during the Albian stage, between 110.1 and 106.3 million years ago.
Gualicho shinyae lived during the Cenomanian stage of the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 93 million years ago, in what is now Argentina.
Gualicho inhabited what is now northern Argentine Patagonia, which was then part of the South American island continent separated from Gondwana.
Fossils of Gualicho were found in the Huincul Formation, dating from the late Cenomanian to early Turonian stages of the Cretaceous, about 93 million years ago.
It has been informally suggested on blogs that Gualicho is synonymous with the megaraptoran Aoniraptor due to similarities in their caudal vertebrae.
A 2020 comparative analysis of pneumatic structures found many differences between Gualicho and Aoniraptor, challenging their synonymy.
In 2025, Calvo and colleagues concluded that Gualicho is not closely related to megaraptorans like Megaraptor due to significant morphological differences in the humerus.
Researchers noted that Gualicho's humerus shares similarities with various coelurosaur groups, making a confident referral to a specific theropod clade difficult.
In 2025, Delcourt et al. recovered Gualicho and Deltadromeus as sister taxa within Ornithomimosauria based on phylogenetic analyses.
Researchers debate whether Gualicho's relatives, the megaraptorans and neovenatorids, were carnosaurs or theropods more closely related to ceratosaurs than to carnosaurs.

Some researchers have suggested that Gualicho might be a synonym of the megaraptoran Aoniraptor, which was found at the Violante site in the Huincul Formation, based on similarities in their tail vertebrae.
Aoniraptor is likely an invalid name (nomen nudum) because it does not meet the requirements of ICZN article 8.5.3.
A 2025 analysis comparing Gualicho's humerus to adult Megaraptor concluded that Gualicho is not closely related to megaraptorans due to significant morphological differences.
